name: AWS CLI
description: Protects against destructive AWS CLI operations like terminate-instances, \ delete-db-instance, s3 rm --recursive, Athena/Glue catalog deletions, and \ destructive Athena queries (DROP, TRUNCATE, DELETE without WHERE)

destructive_patterns.name: ec2-terminate
destructive_patterns.description: aws ec2 terminate-instances permanently destroys EC2 instances.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
terminate-instances permanently destroys EC2 instances:

\ - Instance is stopped and deleted \ - Instance store volumes are lost \ - EBS root volumes deleted (unless DeleteOnTermination=false) \ - Elastic IPs are disassociated

\ This cannot be undone. The instance ID will never be reusable.

\ Preview first: \ aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-xxx

\ Consider stop instead: \ aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-xxx

destructive_patterns.name: removes AWS resources
destructive_patterns.description: aws ec2 delete-* permanently removes AWS resources.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
EC2 delete commands permanently remove resources:

\ - delete-snapshot: Removes EBS snapshot (backup data lost) \ - delete-volume: Destroys EBS volume and all data \ - delete-vpc: Removes VPC (must be empty) \ - delete-image: Deregisters AMI \ - delete-security-group: Removes firewall rules \ - delete-key-pair: Removes SSH key (can't SSH to instances using it)

\ Always verify resource IDs: \ aws ec2 describe-<resource> --<resource>-ids xxx

destructive_patterns.name: s3-rm-recursive
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3 rm --recursive permanently deletes all objects in the path.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
s3 rm --recursive deletes ALL objects under the specified path:

\ - All files and 'folders' are deleted \ - Versioned objects: only current version deleted \ - No trash/recycle bin \ - Cannot be undone (unless versioning enabled)

\ Preview what would be deleted: \ aws s3 ls s3://bucket/path/ --recursive \ aws s3 rm s3://bucket/path/ --recursive --dryrun

\ Consider versioning for recovery: \ aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket bucket

destructive_patterns.name: s3-rb
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3 rb removes the entire S3 bucket.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
s3 rb removes an S3 bucket:

\ - Bucket must be empty (use --force to delete contents first) \ - With --force: deletes all objects then bucket \ - Bucket name becomes available for others \ - Cannot be undone

\ Check bucket contents: \ aws s3 ls s3://bucket --recursive --summarize

\ Verify bucket name: \ aws s3api head-bucket --bucket bucket-name

destructive_patterns.name: s3api-delete-bucket
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3api delete-bucket removes the entire S3 bucket.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
s3api delete-bucket removes a bucket (must be empty):

\ - Returns error if bucket not empty \ - Bucket name released for reuse by anyone \ - Associated policies and configurations lost

\ Empty bucket first if needed: \ aws s3 rm s3://bucket --recursive

\ Or use s3 rb --force for both operations.

destructive_patterns.name: rds-delete
destructive_patterns.description: aws rds delete-* permanently destroys the database resource (instance, cluster, snapshot, parameter group, subnet group, etc.).
destructive_patterns.explanation:
RDS delete commands permanently remove database resources:

\ - delete-db-instance: Destroys the database instance \ - delete-db-cluster: Destroys Aurora cluster \ - delete-db-snapshot: Removes backup \ - delete-db-cluster-snapshot: Removes cluster backup

\ Consider: \ - Create final snapshot before deletion \ - Skip final snapshot only for test instances

\ Create backup: \ aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-id xxx --db-snapshot-id backup

destructive_patterns.name: cfn-delete-stack
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudformation delete-stack removes the entire stack and its resources.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
CloudFormation delete-stack removes the stack AND all resources it created:

\ - EC2 instances terminated \ - RDS databases deleted (unless DeletionPolicy: Retain) \ - S3 buckets removed (if empty) \ - All IAM resources deleted

\ Resources with DeletionPolicy: Retain are kept but orphaned.

\ Preview resources: \ aws cloudformation describe-stack-resources --stack-name xxx

\ Consider: \ aws cloudformation delete-stack --retain-resources res1 res2

destructive_patterns.name: lambda-delete
destructive_patterns.description: aws lambda delete-* permanently removes a Lambda resource (function, alias, layer version, event source mapping, etc.).
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-function removes a Lambda function completely:

\ - Function code is deleted \ - All versions and aliases removed \ - Event source mappings deleted \ - Cannot be undone

\ Backup function code first: \ aws lambda get-function --function-name xxx --query Code.Location

\ List versions: \ aws lambda list-versions-by-function --function-name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: iam-delete
destructive_patterns.description: aws iam delete-* removes IAM resources. Verify dependencies first.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
IAM delete commands remove identity resources:

\ - delete-user: Removes IAM user (must detach policies first) \ - delete-role: Removes role (must detach policies first) \ - delete-policy: Removes managed policy \ - delete-group: Removes IAM group

\ Check dependencies: \ aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name xxx \ aws iam list-entities-for-policy --policy-arn xxx

\ Roles used by services (Lambda, EC2) will break!

destructive_patterns.name: dynamodb-delete
destructive_patterns.description: aws dynamodb delete-table permanently deletes the table and all data.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-table removes a DynamoDB table and ALL its data:

\ - All items are deleted \ - Table configuration is lost \ - Global secondary indexes deleted \ - Cannot be undone

\ Backup first: \ aws dynamodb create-backup --table-name xxx --backup-name backup

\ Or export to S3: \ aws dynamodb export-table-to-point-in-time ...

destructive_patterns.name: eks-delete
destructive_patterns.description: aws eks delete-cluster removes the entire EKS cluster.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-cluster removes an EKS cluster:

\ - Control plane is deleted \ - Node groups must be deleted separately first \ - Kubernetes resources (deployments, services) are lost \ - Persistent volumes may remain as orphaned EBS

\ Delete node groups first: \ aws eks list-nodegroups --cluster-name xxx \ aws eks delete-nodegroup --cluster-name xxx --nodegroup-name yyy

\ Then delete cluster.

destructive_patterns.name: ecr-delete-repository
destructive_patterns.description: aws ecr delete-repository permanently deletes the repository and its images.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-repository removes an ECR repository:

\ - All images in the repository are deleted \ - Repository configuration lost \ - Requires --force if repository not empty

\ List images first: \ aws ecr list-images --repository-name xxx

\ Consider keeping critical images: \ docker pull <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/repo:tag

destructive_patterns.name: ecr-batch-delete-image
destructive_patterns.description: aws ecr batch-delete-image permanently deletes one or more images.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
batch-delete-image removes specific images from ECR:

\ - Images are permanently deleted \ - Can delete by tag or digest \ - Running containers using these images may fail on restart

\ List images: \ aws ecr describe-images --repository-name xxx

\ Verify image usage before deletion.

destructive_patterns.name: ecr-delete-lifecycle-policy
destructive_patterns.description: aws ecr delete-lifecycle-policy removes the repository lifecycle policy.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-lifecycle-policy removes automatic image cleanup rules:

\ - Old images will no longer be automatically deleted \ - May lead to storage cost increases \ - Repository will retain all images indefinitely

\ View current policy: \ aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy --repository-name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: logs-delete-log-group
destructive_patterns.description: aws logs delete-log-group permanently deletes a log group and all events.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-log-group removes a CloudWatch log group:

\ - All log streams are deleted \ - All log events are lost \ - Metric filters and subscriptions removed \ - Cannot be undone

\ Export logs before deletion: \ aws logs create-export-task --log-group-name xxx \ \ --destination bucket --from 0 --to $(date +%s)000

destructive_patterns.name: logs-delete-log-stream
destructive_patterns.description: aws logs delete-log-stream permanently deletes a log stream and all events.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-log-stream removes a specific log stream:

\ - All events in the stream are deleted \ - Log group remains intact \ - Cannot be undone

\ View log stream events before deletion: \ aws logs get-log-events --log-group-name xxx \ \ --log-stream-name yyy --limit 100

destructive_patterns.name: kms-schedule-key-deletion
destructive_patterns.description: aws kms schedule-key-deletion schedules a KMS key for irreversible deletion — all data encrypted with it becomes unreadable.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
schedule-key-deletion starts an irreversible KMS key destruction:

\ - After the waiting period (min 7 days), the key is deleted \ - Every piece of data encrypted under this key becomes \ permanently undecryptable \ - CancelKeyDeletion can abort within the waiting window \ - After deletion: data loss is unrecoverable

\ Prefer `disable-key` if you want to stop usage reversibly: \ aws kms disable-key --key-id xxx

destructive_patterns.name: secretsmanager-delete-secret
destructive_patterns.description: aws secretsmanager delete-secret destroys a stored secret — typically irrecoverable credentials.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-secret removes a Secrets Manager secret:

\ - Default 30-day recovery window unless --force-delete-without-recovery \ - With --force-delete-without-recovery: immediate & unrecoverable \ - All rotation history, versions, and values are lost \ - Credentials for production services can become \ unrecoverable if not backed up

\ Restore during the recovery window: \ aws secretsmanager restore-secret --secret-id xxx

destructive_patterns.name: route53-delete-hosted-zone
destructive_patterns.description: aws route53 delete-hosted-zone removes a DNS zone — domains stop resolving.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-hosted-zone removes a Route53 hosted zone:

\ - All DNS records in the zone are deleted \ - Domains configured with this zone's nameservers stop resolving \ - Production traffic can become unroutable immediately \ - Cannot be undone

\ Export records first: \ aws route53 list-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id xxx > zone-backup.json

destructive_patterns.name: cloudtrail-delete-trail
destructive_patterns.description: aws cloudtrail delete-trail removes an audit trail — compliance/forensics impact.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-trail removes a CloudTrail trail:

\ - Trail configuration is deleted \ - Historical log files in S3 are NOT deleted (still queryable) \ - Future events stop being recorded via this trail \ - Compliance regimes (SOC2, PCI, HIPAA) may require this trail

\ Consider stop-logging if pausing is sufficient: \ aws cloudtrail stop-logging --name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: redshift-delete-cluster
destructive_patterns.description: aws redshift delete-cluster destroys a Redshift cluster and all loaded data.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-cluster removes a Redshift cluster:

\ - With --skip-final-cluster-snapshot: ALL data is destroyed immediately \ - Without --skip-final-cluster-snapshot: cluster deleted after final snapshot \ - Connected BI tools, ETL pipelines, and downstream jobs break \ - Very expensive to restore (hours of snapshot restore)

\ Preview: \ aws redshift describe-clusters --cluster-identifier xxx

destructive_patterns.name: kinesis-delete-stream
destructive_patterns.description: aws kinesis delete-stream destroys a data stream — in-flight records are lost.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-stream removes a Kinesis data stream:

\ - All shards, consumers, and in-flight records are lost \ - Producers and consumers disconnect immediately \ - Data retained only as long as EnhancedMonitoring/FanOut sinks preserved it \ - Stream name is reserved briefly; re-creation may fail until it clears

destructive_patterns.name: efs-delete-file-system
destructive_patterns.description: aws efs delete-file-system destroys an EFS filesystem — all files and mount targets are lost.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-file-system removes an EFS filesystem:

\ - All files in the filesystem are permanently deleted \ - Mount targets and access points are removed \ - Cannot be undone (no built-in recovery) \ - Take a backup first via AWS Backup or rsync out: \ aws backup start-backup-job --backup-vault-name xxx \ \ --resource-arn arn:aws:elasticfilesystem:...:file-system/fs-xxx \ \ --iam-role-arn arn:aws:iam::...:role/backup-role

destructive_patterns.name: s3api-delete-object
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3api delete-object[s]/delete-object-tagging — object(s) or tags are gone unless bucket versioning is enabled.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-object / delete-objects / delete-object-tagging:

\ - Without bucket versioning: objects or tags are permanently gone \ - With versioning (objects only): a delete marker is added; past versions recoverable \ - delete-objects is BATCH (up to 1000 keys per call) — a misfire can wipe thousands \ - No trash/recycle bin

\ Check versioning first: \ aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket xxx

\ Preview the keys about to be deleted: \ aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket xxx --prefix yyy/

destructive_patterns.name: athena-delete-data-catalog
destructive_patterns.description:
aws athena delete-data-catalog removes the data catalog and all \
             database/table definitions tied to it.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-data-catalog detaches and removes an Athena DataCatalog:

\ - All databases and table definitions linked to the catalog are lost \ - Queries referencing this catalog will fail \ - Underlying S3 data is NOT deleted, but becomes unreadable via Athena \ - Cannot be undone (catalog metadata is gone)

\ List catalogs first: \ aws athena list-data-catalogs \ aws athena get-data-catalog --name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: athena-delete-work-group
destructive_patterns.description: aws athena delete-work-group removes the Athena workgroup and its configuration.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-work-group removes an Athena workgroup:

\ - Query history, IAM-scoped configuration, and cost controls are lost \ - In-flight queries are cancelled \ - With --recursive-delete-option, named queries in the workgroup are also dropped

\ Preview first: \ aws athena get-work-group --work-group xxx

destructive_patterns.name: athena-delete-named-query
destructive_patterns.description: aws athena delete-named-query permanently removes a saved query.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-named-query deletes a saved Athena query:

\ - The stored query text and metadata are removed \ - No data is lost, but the query must be rewritten from scratch if \ it wasn't stored elsewhere

\ Retrieve the query before deleting: \ aws athena get-named-query --named-query-id xxx

destructive_patterns.name: athena-query-drop-database
destructive_patterns.description: Athena DROP DATABASE/SCHEMA removes the database from the Glue catalog.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
DROP DATABASE/SCHEMA removes a database from the Glue catalog:

\ - All table definitions inside the database are lost \ - Queries referencing this database will fail \ - Underlying S3 data is NOT deleted, just unreadable via Athena \ - Cannot be undone (catalog metadata lost)

\ List tables first: \ aws athena start-query-execution \ \ --query-string 'SHOW TABLES IN database_name'

\ For more control, use `aws glue delete-database` \ (which this pack also blocks).

destructive_patterns.name: athena-query-drop-table
destructive_patterns.description: Athena DROP TABLE/VIEW removes the table definition from the Glue catalog.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
DROP TABLE/VIEW removes a table or view from the catalog:

\ - Table definition is lost \ - Queries referencing this table will fail \ - Underlying S3 data is NOT deleted

\ Preview schema first: \ aws athena start-query-execution \ \ --query-string 'SHOW CREATE TABLE db.table'

destructive_patterns.name: athena-query-truncate
destructive_patterns.description: Athena TRUNCATE TABLE deletes all rows from an Iceberg table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
TRUNCATE TABLE in Athena (Iceberg tables):

\ - All rows are deleted from the table \ - The table definition is preserved \ - Underlying S3 objects are removed for Iceberg tables \ - Cannot be undone (no implicit snapshot retention)

\ Consider a targeted DELETE with WHERE clause instead.

destructive_patterns.name: athena-query-string-from-file
destructive_patterns.description: Athena --query-string loaded from file:// or fileb:// — SQL content is opaque to the guard.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Athena `start-query-execution --query-string file://…` loads the \ SQL from disk, so the engine can't inspect the statement. The file may \ contain DROP DATABASE, TRUNCATE TABLE, or an unscoped DELETE.

\ Prefer the inline form so the guard can see what you're running: \ aws athena start-query-execution \ \ --query-string 'SELECT … FROM …'

\ If a file-loaded query is genuinely required, cat it first so \ the content is inspectable, and allowlist this rule in your \ project the engine config with a justification.

destructive_patterns.name: athena-cli-input-file
destructive_patterns.description: Athena --cli-input-json/yaml loaded from file:// or fileb:// — content is opaque to the guard.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`--cli-input-json file://…` (or `-yaml`) supplies the whole \ invocation — including QueryString — from a file on disk. the engine \ only greps the command line, so a DROP or TRUNCATE buried in \ the JSON/YAML body on disk slips past every other Athena rule.

\ Inline JSON/YAML (e.g. `--cli-input-json '{…}'`) is still \ allowed because the engine can read the literal in the command line \ and catch a DROP there.

\ Prefer explicit `--query-string '…'`, or inline the JSON blob. \ If the file-backed form is genuinely required, allowlist this \ rule with a justification.

destructive_patterns.name: athena-query-delete-without-where
destructive_patterns.description: Athena DELETE without a WHERE clause removes all rows from the target table.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
DELETE FROM <table> without a WHERE clause:

\ - Every row in the table is deleted \ - Iceberg tables: underlying S3 data is dropped \ - Hive tables: operation fails (Athena rejects unscoped DELETE on Hive) \ - Cannot be undone (no automatic snapshots)

\ Rewrite with a WHERE clause that scopes the deletion: \ DELETE FROM db.table WHERE <predicate>

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-database
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue delete-database removes the database and every table definition inside it.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-database drops a Glue database and every table/partition in it:

\ - All table definitions in the database are lost \ - Athena / EMR / Redshift Spectrum queries referencing these tables will fail \ - Underlying S3 data is preserved, but becomes unreadable via the catalog \ - Cannot be undone (metadata is gone)

\ List tables first: \ aws glue get-tables --database-name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-table
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue delete-table removes the table definition from the catalog.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-table removes a Glue table definition:

\ - Table schema and partition metadata are lost \ - Underlying S3 data is NOT deleted \ - Queries referencing this table will fail

\ Preview the table first: \ aws glue get-table --database-name xxx --name yyy

destructive_patterns.name: glue-batch-delete-table
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue batch-delete-table removes multiple table definitions in one call.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
batch-delete-table drops several Glue tables in one API call:

\ - All listed table definitions are lost \ - Underlying S3 data is preserved \ - Queries referencing these tables will fail \ - Cannot be undone

\ Review the exact names first: \ aws glue get-tables --database-name xxx

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-partition
destructive_patterns.description:
aws glue delete-partition removes partition metadata; the partition is no longer \
             queryable until recreated.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-partition removes a Glue partition's metadata:

\ - Partition metadata is lost (column stats, location pointer) \ - Underlying S3 data is preserved \ - Queries scoped to that partition will return no rows until re-registered

destructive_patterns.name: glue-batch-delete-partition
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue batch-delete-partition removes multiple partition definitions in one call.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
batch-delete-partition drops several Glue partitions at once:

\ - Every listed partition's metadata is lost \ - Underlying S3 data is preserved \ - Recreate via `aws glue batch-create-partition` if you still have the list

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-crawler
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue delete-crawler removes the crawler configuration.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-crawler removes a Glue crawler:

\ - Crawler configuration (targets, schedule, schema detection rules) is lost \ - Schedules and classifiers tied to the crawler are orphaned \ - Can be re-created from Infrastructure-as-Code if present

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-job
destructive_patterns.description: aws glue delete-job removes the ETL job definition and all of its run history.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-job removes a Glue ETL job:

\ - Job script reference, connections, arguments, and schedule are lost \ - All run history and metrics for the job are removed \ - Scheduled triggers referencing the job will fail

\ Export the job definition first: \ aws glue get-job --job-name xxx > job-backup.json

destructive_patterns.name: glue-delete-dev-endpoint
destructive_patterns.description:
aws glue delete-dev-endpoint tears down the development endpoint and any attached \
             SageMaker notebook configuration.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
delete-dev-endpoint shuts down a Glue DevEndpoint:

\ - Endpoint is stopped and deleted \ - Attached SageMaker notebook (if any) must be cleaned up separately \ - Ongoing sessions / jobs on the endpoint are terminated
